title: Reading 19th-century non-fiction
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: the 19th-century source, which the specification sets in every series

tips.title: Find the spine
tips.body: Subject and main verb first; turn an inversion round; read joint by joint at the semicolons. A Victorian sentence is a short main clause with a great deal hung on it.

tips.title: Read the gloss first
tips.body: The insert introduces each source with its date and context and glosses in brackets the words the examiners judge unfamiliar. Wharf in June 2024. Read it before the source, not after.

tips.title: Praise that means its opposite
tips.body: Nice, gentlemanly, noble creatures: when a Victorian writer praises the people who refused her, the praise is irony and the reader is being asked to judge. Name it as a method with its effect.

tips.title: The same convention, used oppositely
tips.body: Direct address makes Seacole's reader a judge and Nightingale's an agent. A convention shared by two texts and used differently is a Question 4 comparison ready made.

tips.title: One sentence of period
tips.body: Written in 1857 by a woman of colour refused by the War Office, the irony is the weapon the form allowed. Tied to a method, the period explains a choice; on its own it is history.

tips.title: Never old-fashioned
tips.body: The word tells the examiner you have stopped reading. Restraint, formality and address to the reader are choices, and what a Victorian writer will not say is often the loudest thing in the passage.

why.matters: Half of every Paper 2 is written by someone who died more than a century ago, and the paper pairs it with a modern text on purpose: to see how a perspective is shaped by its time, and how the same conventions, addressing the reader, restraint, irony, do different work in different hands. Reading a Victorian sentence for its spine, a Victorian word from the job it does, and a Victorian convention as a method is a skill that unlocks most of the writing there is, since most of it is old, and it is the skill that lets a reader hear a woman the War Office turned away in 1854 say, without one accusing word, exactly what was done to her.

examples.title: Everything written before you
examples.body: Letters in a family, the founding documents of a country, the speeches in a history lesson, the novels on the Literature paper: most of what is worth reading was written in sentences longer than ours, by people who addressed their readers directly and left the loudest things unsaid. The habits of this topic, spine, words, conventions, period, are the habits that make all of it readable, and readable as choices rather than as quaintness.

examples.title: Hearing what could not be said
examples.body: Seacole could not write, in 1857, that she was refused for the colour of her skin, so she wrote irony and restraint and let the reader say it. Writers under every kind of constraint, censorship, politeness, fear, have done the same, and the reader who can hear the loud silence in a Victorian memoir can hear it in a modern press statement or a carefully worded apology. The period teaches the method, and the method is everywhere.

steps.title: One source will always be from the 19th century
steps.body:
The specification says the Paper 2 sources will be drawn from the 19th century and from either the 20th or 21st, so that viewpoints can be compared over time, and it lists the kinds of text: journalism, articles, reports, essays, travel writing, accounts, sketches, letters, diaries, autobiography and biographical passages. In June 2024 the 19th-century source was Mary Seacole's memoir of 1857.

**What is different about it.** Longer sentences, held together with semicolons and dashes; a formal register; words that have shifted or gone; conventions that look odd now, such as addressing the reader directly or framing an experience as a moral lesson. None of it is an obstacle once the habits are known, and the insert helps: it introduces each source with its date and context, and glosses hard words in brackets, as the June 2024 insert explained *wharf*.

**What is the same.** The questions. The 19th-century source is read for its perspective and its methods like any other, and it is often the source with the richer language.

rows: Tells a life, and shapes it
Argues a case, sets out findings
Speaks to one reader, or to nobody
Any of the thousands the period kept
Reports a place or an event to readers at home

steps.title: The sentences are longer: how to read them
steps.body:
A Victorian sentence can run for six lines, and the way in is always the same: find the main verb and its subject, and read the rest as things hung on them.

**Inversion.** “Many a long hour did I wait in his great hall”, Seacole writes, and the verb comes before its subject, *did I wait*, for emphasis. Turn it round, *I waited many a long hour*, and the sentence is plain.

**Semicolons and dashes.** They mark the joints. Read to the first semicolon, understand that, then read on. A pair of dashes holds an aside that can be skipped on a first read and returned to.

**Parenthesis in the middle.** *Many of them looking curiously at me* is hung on *scores passed in and out*. The main clause is usually short; the length is in what is attached.

**The habit.** Read the long sentence twice: once to find the spine, once for the rest. The 15 minutes at the start of the paper are for this.

rows: Many a long hour did I wait in his great hall, while scores passed in and out; many of them looking curiously at me.
How long; where; what happened meanwhile; how they looked
So I made long and unwearied application at the War Office, in blissful ignorance of the labour and time I was throwing away.
How; where; in what state of mind

steps.title: Vocabulary: from the context, from the gloss, and on
steps.body:
Old or formal words are guessed from the job they do in the sentence, and the guess is usually enough.

**From the job.** Seacole lays a “pertinacious siege” to the Secretary-at-War's house: a siege is laid to something that will not open, and *pertinacious*, whatever it means exactly, describes how she lays it, so the sense is stubborn, persistent, and the sentence reads. The “The flunkeys, noble creatures!” who resent her are servants in livery, from the way they behave; the word need not be known.

**From the gloss.** The insert explains what the examiners judge a student cannot be expected to know: *wharf* in June 2024, with its definition in the introduction to the source. Read the gloss before the source.

**From the shifted meaning.** Some words have moved: *nice* meant precise or particular as often as pleasant, and Seacole's {SE_FELLOWS} are not being praised.

**And on.** A word that will not give up its meaning is left, and the sentence read for its spine. The questions never turn on one obscure word.

rows: A siege is laid to something that will not open
They resent her, marvel at her, show their sovereign will
She attached herself to another department with it

check.solution: The job the word does in its sentence gives its sense: she besieges the house as she besieged the office, refusing to be sent away. Exactness is not needed; the sentence reads once the spine and the sense are in place.

steps.title: The practice text: Seacole at the War Office
steps.body:
In 1854, before she went to the Crimea, Mary Seacole offered herself in London as a nurse and was refused. This is her account of it, written three years later, as she wrote it.

> So I made long and unwearied application at the War Office, in blissful ignorance of the labour and time I was throwing away. I have reason to believe that I considerably interfered with the repose of sundry messengers, and disturbed, to an alarming degree, the official gravity of some nice gentlemanly young fellows, who were working out their salaries in an easy, off-hand way. But my ridiculous endeavours to gain an interview with the Secretary-at-War of course failed, and glad at last to oblige a distracted messenger, I transferred my attentions to the Quartermaster-General's department. Here I saw another gentleman, who listened to me with a great deal of polite enjoyment, and—his amusement ended—hinted, had I not better apply to the Medical Department; and accordingly I attached myself to their quarters with the same unwearying ardour. But, of course, I grew tired at last, and then I changed my plans.

> Now, I am not for a single instant going to blame the authorities who would not listen to the offer of a motherly yellow woman to go to the Crimea and nurse her "sons" there, suffering from cholera, diarrhoea, and a host of lesser ills. In my country, where people know our use, it would have been different; but here it was natural enough—although I had references, and other voices spoke for me—that they should laugh, good-naturedly enough, at my offer. War, I know, is a serious game, but sometimes very humble actors are of great use in it, and if the reader, when he comes in time to peruse the evidence of those who had to do with the Sebastopol drama, of my share in it, will turn back to this chapter, he will confess perhaps that, after all, the impulse which led me to the War Department was not unnatural.

> My new scheme was, I candidly confess, worse devised than the one which had failed. Miss Nightingale had left England for the Crimea, but other nurses were still to follow, and my new plan was simply to offer myself to Mrs. H—— as a recruit. Feeling that I was one of the very women they most wanted, experienced and fond of the work, I jumped at once to the conclusion that they would gladly enrol me in their number. To go to Cox's, the army agents, who were most obliging to me, and obtain the Secretary-at-War's private address, did not take long; and that done, I laid the same pertinacious siege to his great house in —— Square, as I had previously done to his place of business.

> Many a long hour did I wait in his great hall, while scores passed in and out; many of them looking curiously at me. The flunkeys, noble creatures! marvelled exceedingly at the yellow woman whom no excuses could get rid of, nor impertinence dismay, and showed me very clearly that they resented my persisting in remaining there in mute appeal from their sovereign will. At last I gave that up, after a message from Mrs. H. that the full complement of nurses had been secured, and that my offer could not be entertained. Once again I tried, and had an interview this time with one of Miss Nightingale's companions. She gave me the same reply, and I read in her face the fact, that had there been a vacancy, I should not have been chosen to fill it.

**What to notice.** The irony: the “nice gentlemanly young fellows” “working out their salaries in an easy, off-hand way”, and “The flunkeys, noble creatures!” with its exclamation mark, praise that means its opposite. The direct address to *the reader*, who is asked to turn back to this chapter later and judge. The refusal to blame, which is itself a way of blaming. And the last sentence, “I read in her face the fact, that had there been a vacancy, I should not have been chosen to fill it.”, where the restraint does the work: she does not say why, and the reader knows.

Praise that means its opposite; the reader is invited to smile with her
if the reader … will turn back to this chapter
The reader made a judge of her case
I am not for a single instant going to blame the authorities
A blame that is stronger for being withheld

steps.title: A Question 3 paragraph on Seacole's irony
steps.body: Suppose Question 3 asks how the writer uses language to describe the people who refused her. Here is a Level 4 paragraph on the irony.

visuals.problem: Write a Level 4 paragraph on how Seacole uses language to describe the officials.

steps.text: Choose two details that work together: the “nice gentlemanly young fellows” “working out their salaries in an easy, off-hand way”, and “The flunkeys, noble creatures!”.
steps.note: Two ironies that build one impression of the people who refused her.

steps.text: Name the choice: irony, praise that means its opposite, carried by the adjectives nice and gentlemanly and by an exclamation of mock admiration.
steps.note: Exact terms: irony; mock admiration; the adjectives; the exclamation.

steps.text: Effect on the reader: the reader is invited to smile with the writer at men who are described as exactly what they are not, and the smile is a judgement the writer never has to state.
steps.note: Effect, and the reason the words produce it: the reader does the judging.

steps.text: Extend with the voice: she claims not to blame them, “I am not for a single instant going to blame the authorities”, and the claim, placed after the irony, is one more irony, so that the refusal to blame becomes the strongest blame in the passage.
steps.note: A second choice that extends the first: the voice as a method.

steps.text: Finish on what the writer wants: a reader who has laughed at the officials and then reads, in the last sentence, why she was refused, has been led to a judgement about prejudice without a single accusing word.
steps.note: What the writer wants the reader to feel about the real thing, and how the passage earns it.

check.prompt: Why is Seacole's refusal to blame the authorities read as irony?
check.solution: Placement makes the irony: the reader has just been invited to smile at the officials, and is about to be told what the refusal was really for. A refusal to blame in that position is a way of blaming that leaves the writer clean. That is a method read in context.

steps.title: A second 19th-century voice: Nightingale argues
steps.body:
Two years after Seacole's memoir, Florence Nightingale published *Notes on Nursing*, an essay rather than a story. Its preface is a different 19th-century voice, and a natural partner for Question 4.

> The following notes are by no means intended as a rule of thought by which nurses can teach themselves to nurse, still less as a manual to teach nurses to nurse. They are meant simply to give hints for thought to women who have personal charge of the health of others. Every woman, or at least almost every woman, in England has, at one time or another of her life, charge of the personal health of somebody, whether child or invalid,—in other words, every woman is a nurse. Every day sanitary knowledge, or the knowledge of nursing, or in other words, of how to put the constitution in such a state as that it will have no disease, or that it can recover from disease, takes a higher place. It is recognized as the knowledge which every one ought to have—distinct from medical knowledge, which only a profession can have.

> If, then, every woman must at some time or other of her life, become a nurse, i.e., have charge of somebody's health, how immense and how valuable would be the produce of her united experience if every woman would think how to nurse.

> I do not pretend to teach her how, I ask her to teach herself, and for this purpose I venture to give her some hints.

**What to notice.** The definition by repetition, “every woman is a nurse”, reached by a chain of *every woman* and an *in other words*. The reasoning structure, “If, then, every woman must at some time or other of her life, become a nurse”, which is the shape of an argument, if then, in a Victorian sentence. The direct address, “I do not pretend to teach her how, I ask her to teach herself”, which makes the reader the agent. And the modesty that is a claim: the notes are only “hints for thought”, and a whole book of instruction follows them.

**Against Seacole.** Both women claim, in the 1850s, that nursing is knowledge and that women hold it; Seacole claims it by telling what she did and how she was refused, Nightingale by defining what a nurse is and asking every woman to become one. Story against argument: a Question 4 comparison in one sentence.

Essay: an argument about what should be
Nursing is what she does and was refused for

steps.title: Untangle, then read
steps.body:
Take these two sentences. For each, find the spine, then read the rest as things hung on it, then say in one plain sentence what it means.

1. Seacole: *I have reason to believe that I considerably interfered with the repose of sundry messengers, and disturbed, to an alarming degree, the official gravity of some nice gentlemanly young fellows, who were working out their salaries in an easy, off-hand way.*
2. Nightingale: *It is recognized as the knowledge which every one ought to have, distinct from medical knowledge, which only a profession can have.*

Then, for each, name one method and its effect, as you would for Question 3.

steps.title: Reading the period as perspective
steps.body:
The habits of Victorian writing, addressing the reader, framing a life as a lesson, formality, restraint, are not obstacles to be got past; they are the writer's choices, and they carry the perspective.

**Direct address as a method.** Seacole makes the reader a judge; Nightingale makes the reader an agent. The convention is the same and the use is opposite, and that is a Question 4 comparison.

**Restraint as a method.** A Victorian writer who will not say a thing is often saying it as loudly as the form allows. Seacole reads a refusal in a face and stops; the modern reader who calls that old-fashioned reticence has missed the loudest sentence in the passage.

**The period in a sentence.** Written in 1857 by a woman who had been refused by the War Office, the memoir's irony is the only weapon a Victorian woman of colour could use in print against the men who refused her. One sentence, tied to a method, and the period has explained a choice. A paragraph of history would not.

**Never old-fashioned.** The word tells the examiner the reader has stopped reading. The 19th-century source is read as a writer's choices, and its difference from the modern source is the point of the paper.

steps.title: The 19th-century source in one page
steps.body:
Every Paper 2 has one, and it is read like any other source, with three extra habits.

- **The kinds:** journalism, essays, travel writing, letters, diaries, memoir; the insert gives the date, the context and a gloss for hard words.
- **Long sentences:** find the spine, subject and main verb; turn inversions round; read joint by joint at the semicolons and dashes.
- **Words:** from the job they do; from the gloss; from shifted meanings such as nice; then on, because no question turns on one word.
- **Conventions are methods:** direct address makes the reader a judge or an agent; restraint says loudly what the form will not; irony is praise that means its opposite.
- **The period in a sentence,** tied to a method, explaining a choice; never the word old-fashioned.
- **The pair:** Seacole's story against Nightingale's argument, both claiming nursing as women's knowledge in the 1850s.

The 19th-century source is often the richer of the two, and the one the period difference is there to explain.

questions.prompt: What is the term for praise that means its opposite, as in nice gentlemanly young fellows?
questions.solution: Irony: saying the opposite of what is meant so that the reader supplies the judgement. Seacole's memoir runs on it, because it was the weapon the form allowed a Victorian woman of colour against the men who refused her.

markScheme.description: irony

questions.prompt: Nightingale writes that she does not pretend to teach her how, but asks her to teach herself. What does the direct address do here, compared with Seacole's?
questions.solution: Both writers address a reader, and the uses are opposite: judge my case; teach yourself. A convention shared by two texts and used differently is the best kind of Question 4 comparison, because the method is the same and the perspective is not.

markScheme.description: It makes the reader an agent who must act, where Seacole's makes the reader a judge; the same convention, used oppositely

options: It is not direct address, because the reader is called her rather than you
It makes the reader an agent who must act, where Seacole's makes the reader a judge; the same convention, used oppositely
It is exactly the same use of direct address as Seacole's, since both writers address a reader and both were nurses
It shows that Nightingale did not know how to nurse

questions.prompt: Why is the last sentence of the Seacole passage, in which she reads the refusal in a face, the loudest in the passage?
questions.solution: What a Victorian writer will not say is often said loudest by the form: she reads it in a face and stops, and the reader, who has been shown everything, finishes the sentence. Restraint is a method, and this is its effect.

markScheme.description: Because the restraint makes the reader supply the reason, after the passage has shown her laughed at, so the prejudice is stated by the reader

options: Because it names Miss Nightingale, the most famous person in the passage
Because it is the longest sentence in the passage and the one with the most clauses in it
Because the restraint makes the reader supply the reason, after the passage has shown her laughed at, so the prejudice is stated by the reader
Because it is the only sentence in the whole passage in which Seacole raises her voice and says plainly what she thinks of the people who refused her

questions.prompt: Which sentence compares the two 19th-century writers' perspectives and methods in one move?
questions.solution: The sentence about story against argument holds both writers on one idea with a difference, names a method in each and says what each does to the reader: judge against recruit. The others state dates, a preference, or a similarity without method.

markScheme.description: Both claim nursing as women's knowledge: Seacole by telling how she was refused, with irony that makes the reader her judge; Nightingale by defining a nurse, with repetition that recruits

options: Seacole wrote in 1857 and Nightingale in 1859, so they are both 19th-century writers and can be compared for that reason alone
Seacole is more interesting than Nightingale because her passage has more happening in it, with officials, servants and a great house, where Nightingale only has ideas
Both writers were nurses and both wrote books about it in the same decade, so their perspectives on nursing must be very similar
Both claim nursing as women's knowledge: Seacole by telling how she was refused, with irony that makes the reader her judge; Nightingale by defining a nurse, with repetition that recruits

questions.prompt: What is the word for a sentence in which the verb comes before its subject for emphasis, as in Many a long hour did I wait?
questions.solution: Inversion: the verb before the subject, did I wait, so that the length of the waiting comes first. Turn it round to read it, and name it as a choice when it does something, as it does here.

markScheme.description: inversion

questions.prompt: Put these four sentences in the order that builds a Level 4 point on Seacole's refusal to blame.
questions.solution: The choice quoted, its placement, the effect the placement produces, and what the writer wants the reader to conclude. A method read in context, from the words to the reader.

markScheme.description: the four sentences in order

items: Seacole announces that she is not for a single instant going to blame the authorities
The refusal comes directly after two ironies at the officials' expense, the gentlemanly young fellows and the noble flunkeys
Placed there, the refusal to blame is heard as one more irony, and the strongest blame in the passage
The reader, who has laughed at the officials and is about to learn why she was refused, is led to a judgement about prejudice without one accusing word

questions.prompt: How does Seacole use language to describe the people who refused her? Write a full Question 3 answer on the War Office passage, of about the length you would write for twelve marks.
questions.solution: Seacole's method is irony, and its effect is to make the reader her judge without her ever having to accuse anyone. The men at the War Office are “nice gentlemanly young fellows” who are “working out their salaries in an easy, off-hand way”: every adjective is praise, and every one means its opposite, so that the reader smiles at men described as exactly what they are not and the smile is a judgement the writer never states. The servants who resent her waiting are “The flunkeys, noble creatures!”, and the exclamation mark makes the mock admiration audible; the sentence honours them in the words that mock them. Then she claims not to blame the authorities, “I am not for a single instant going to blame the authorities”, and placed after two ironies, and before the reason she was refused, the claim is one more irony, the strongest blame in the passage delivered as a refusal to blame. She calls herself “a motherly yellow woman”, giving the reader the word the officials were thinking, and in the final sentence she reads the refusal in a companion's face, “I read in her face the fact, that had there been a vacancy, I should not have been chosen to fill it.”, and stops. The restraint is the loudest choice in the passage: the reader, who has been shown the laughter and the word, finishes the sentence with the prejudice she will not name. What Seacole wants is a reader who has been led, by irony and by what is left unsaid, to conclude what a Victorian woman of colour could not say in print, and who will turn back to this chapter, as she asks, to judge.

questions.prompt: Compare how Seacole and Nightingale convey their different perspectives on women as nurses. Refer to the War Office passage and the preface to Notes on Nursing. Write two Question 4 paragraphs: both writers in the first sentence of each, a method from each set against the other, and a difference sharpened, with the period in a sentence where the texts show it.
questions.solution:
Both women claim, within two years of each other, that nursing is knowledge and that women hold it, but Seacole makes the claim by telling how she was refused and Nightingale by defining what a nurse is. Seacole's method is irony: the “nice gentlemanly young fellows” who laughed at her offer are praised in words that mean their opposite, and the reader, invited to smile, does the judging she will not do in her own voice. Nightingale's method is definition by repetition: “every woman is a nurse” arrives at the end of a chain of every woman and in other words, so that a reader who is a woman is inside the claim before it is made. Where Seacole's perspective is a grievance turned into a case, Nightingale's is a principle turned into an instruction, and the difference of method is the difference of purpose: one wants a verdict, the other wants recruits.

Both address the reader directly, and the same convention does opposite work. Seacole asks the reader to turn back to this chapter after reading of her share in the Crimea, making the reader a judge who will weigh the refusal against what she did; Nightingale writes “I do not pretend to teach her how, I ask her to teach herself”, making the reader an agent who must act. Both also use restraint, differently: Seacole reads the true reason for her refusal in a face and stops, so that the prejudice a Victorian woman of colour could not name in print is named by the reader; Nightingale calls a whole book of instruction “hints for thought”, a modesty that is itself a claim to authority. Written in 1857 and 1859, both books use the forms the period allowed a woman, the memoir and the improving essay, to say what the War Office would not hear; for Seacole nursing is what she did and was refused for, and for Nightingale it is what every woman already is, and the reader of both finishes knowing which writer wanted to be judged and which wanted to be obeyed.

questions.prompt: A student writes: 'Seacole's writing is old-fashioned and hard to read, so her perspective is less clear than a modern writer's.' What is the better account?
questions.solution: Old-fashioned tells the examiner the reader has stopped. The period is a set of choices, and the paper pairs the sources so that those choices can be compared with modern ones. A Victorian irony read as a method is as clear as a modern joke.

markScheme.description: The conventions of her period, irony, address and restraint, are her methods, and read as choices they convey a perspective precisely

options: The conventions of her period, irony, address and restraint, are her methods, and read as choices they convey a perspective precisely
Seacole's writing is not old-fashioned because she was ahead of her time
The word old-fashioned is a technical term the examiners reward
The student is right, and the modern source should be preferred for every question that allows a choice of source

questions.prompt: Why is Nightingale's modesty, calling her book only hints for thought, worth analysing as a method?
questions.solution: Modesty is a register, and register is a choice. The preface disclaims teaching and then teaches; the reader is disarmed before being instructed. Reading the disclaimer as a method, and saying what it does, is what turns a convention into analysis.

markScheme.description: Because the modesty is a claim to authority: a writer who offers only hints and then writes a whole book of instruction has made the reader accept it

options: Because it shows that Nightingale did not think her book was any good and expected nobody to read it
Because the modesty is a claim to authority: a writer who offers only hints and then writes a whole book of instruction has made the reader accept it
Because modesty was compulsory for women writers in the 19th century, so a modest preface was expected of Nightingale and cannot be read as a choice she made
Because it proves the book was never meant to be read

examTechnique.body:
**One source is always 19th-century.** Read the insert's introduction and gloss first; they give the date, the context and the hard words.

**Long sentences:** find the spine, subject and main verb, turn inversions round, read joint by joint. Twice, in the 15 minutes.

**Words:** from the job they do, from the gloss, from a shifted meaning; then move on. No question turns on one word.

**Conventions are methods:** irony, direct address, restraint, definition, modesty. Name each with its effect, as on any source.

**The period in a sentence,** tied to a choice, in Question 4 especially: it is why the perspectives differ. Never the word old-fashioned.
examinerErrors: Calling the 19th-century source old-fashioned, difficult or boring, which is a reader stopping rather than an analysis.
Missing irony and reading Victorian praise as sincere.
Getting lost in a long sentence and quoting a fragment that means the opposite of the whole.
Treating direct address or restraint as quaintness rather than as methods with effects.
A paragraph of Victorian history in Question 4, instead of a sentence of period tied to a choice.
Stopping at an unknown word, when the gloss or the sentence's job would have given its sense.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 reader takes the 19th-century source as the richer of the two: finds the spine of each long sentence and reads the rest as attachments, takes the hard words from the job they do and moves on, and reads every convention of the period as a choice. Irony is named and its effect on the reader given; direct address is read for what it makes the reader, a judge or an agent; restraint is heard as the loudest thing in the passage. In Question 4 the period explains a difference in one sentence tied to a method, and the two writers' perspectives are set against each other as story against argument, verdict against recruit.
